title: PowerShell Script Blocks Containing Base64 Decode Calls
exclusions: Detects Event 4104 fragments whose `ScriptBlockText` contains `FromBase64String` or its reversed spelling, following the cited Splunk analytic. It does not prove decoded content is malicious, decode/execute payloads, detect every encoding/obfuscation method, reassemble split script blocks, cover disabled/missing logging, Windows PowerShell versus PowerShell Core channel drift, or establish parent process/network behavior. Script Block Logging records processed content but a match can be legitimate administration or software. No automated blocking, runtime validation, regulatory assurance, or SME sign-off is claimed.
evidence: Retain `windows_powershell_4104_base64_decode`, ACL/schedule/dispatch/alert history, each row's host/user/script-block ID/path/fragment numbers/text hash/preview/record ID, restricted raw 4104 XML and reconstructed script when authorized, effective policy, source coverage, add-on versions, controls, analyst disposition, and bounded exception. This review executed no PowerShell, decode, search, or alert.

controlTest.positiveScenario: Insert one XML 4104 event in the closed window with source `XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational`, host `WS01`, ScriptBlockId `11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111`, MessageNumber/Total 1, and ScriptBlockText `[Convert]::FromBase64String('VGVzdA==')`. Expect one row with `match_type=frombase64string`, correct IDs, and a SHA-256 text hash; no payload execution.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Expect zero rows for benign 4104 `Get-Process`, Event 4103, wrong channel, empty text, qualifying text in newest excluded five minutes, and string `ToBase64String`. Confirm a reversed `gnirtS46esaBmorF` fixture is separately labelled `reversed_frombase64string`.

dataSources: Windows PowerShell Script Block Logging Event 4104 from `Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational` (and a separately validated PowerShell Core source if adopted), collected with Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (Splunkbase 742) as `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog`, `source=XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational`, deployment-local `index=wineventlog`. Required fields: `_time`, `Computer`/`host`, `EventCode`, `EventRecordID`, `ScriptBlockText`, `ScriptBlockId`, `MessageNumber`, `MessageTotal`, `Path`, `UserID`/`user_id`, and `ProcessID`.
app: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742), reviewed at 10.0.1. Splunk Security Content supplies the analytic precedent; Enterprise Security is optional.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog" source="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational" EventCode=4104 earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m ScriptBlockText=*
| eval event_id=tonumber(coalesce(EventCode,EventID)), host=lower(trim(coalesce(Computer,dest,host))), script_text=ScriptBlockText
| where event_id=4104 AND len(host)>0 AND len(script_text)>0 AND (match(script_text,"(?i)frombase64string") OR match(script_text,"(?i)gnirts46esabmorf"))
| eval match_type=case(match(script_text,"(?i)frombase64string"),"frombase64string",match(script_text,"(?i)gnirts46esabmorf"),"reversed_frombase64string"), script_text_sha256=sha256(script_text), script_preview=substr(replace(script_text,"[\r\n]+"," "),1,240), user=lower(trim(coalesce(user_id,UserID,UserName,"unknown")))
| table _time host user match_type ScriptBlockId MessageNumber MessageTotal Path ProcessID script_text_sha256 script_preview EventRecordID source sourcetype
| sort 0 -_time host ScriptBlockId
description: Reports one row for each closed-window PowerShell 4104 fragment containing a direct or reversed `FromBase64String` token. The result preserves host, user, script-block/fragment identity, path, process, cryptographic text hash, bounded preview, event identity, and match type for security triage.
value: Base64 decoding is common but also frequently used by loaders and fileless tradecraft. Script-block content gives defenders a direct, de-obfuscated observation point; retaining fragment identity and hashes lets analysts correlate code across hosts, separate software deployment from abuse, and pivot to process/network evidence without executing unknown payloads. This improves script triage by preserving decoded-operation context instead of treating all Base64 use as malicious.
implementation: Enable Script Block Logging through governed Windows PowerShell policy, collect the Operational channel as XML, and validate 4104 fields/source. Save `windows_powershell_4104_base64_decode`, run every five minutes over the preceding delayed bucket, and alert on any row. Restrict script content, reassemble fragments only in a controlled workflow, and correlate user/process/parent/network/signature before containment.
visualization: Show PowerShell source coverage first, then matches by host/user/path, a timeline, repeated text hashes, and restricted preview table. Drilldown to exact fragments and correlated process/network/EDR records; never render or execute decoded content in dashboards.
dataModelAcceleration: No Change CIM substitute preserves ScriptBlockText and fragment identity. Summary indexing must protect sensitive code and prove event/hash parity.

knownFalsePositives:
A token match is real; intent remains unknown.

1. **Microsoft Configuration Manager CMPivot/Run Scripts** — Match `C:\Windows\CCM\ScriptStore`, SCCM operation ID, administrator and target collection. Use an expiring path/hash/job exception only after review.

2. **Azure DevOps/Jenkins/Octopus deployment** — Installers often decode certificates/configuration. Verify signed pipeline, repository revision, service account, host and UTC window.

3. **Microsoft Exchange/SharePoint/Azure modules** — Vendor modules may decode legitimate values. Validate module path/signature/version and exact hash; avoid broad module-name allowlists.

4. **Defender/EDR response or forensic collection** — Confirm case, responder, live-response audit and script hash; preserve alert as evidence.

5. **Atomic Red Team/purple-team T1059.001 test** — Match engagement, operator, source script/hash and timebox.

**Safe suppression:** post-result `lookup windows_powershell_4104_exceptions.csv` by exact `script_text_sha256,Path,host,exception_id` with owner/approver/reason and numeric validity bounds. Reject wildcards/open-ended entries.
hardware: Windows endpoints/servers running Windows PowerShell with Script Block Logging. PowerShell Core uses a distinct channel/provider that requires separate validation.
reviewer: documentation-only Cursor AI editorial review against Microsoft PowerShell logging/policy documentation, Splunk Windows add-on and Security Content, and MITRE ATT&CK; policy, event generation, fragments, SPL, controls, alerts, decoding, and response not executed or SME-signed

cost.search_load_notes: Search is narrow, but 4104 script content can be high-volume and sensitive; invocation logging adds substantial volume and is not required.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and contract

Assign endpoint policy, PowerShell, Splunk, SOC/privacy and exception owners. Inventory Windows PowerShell and PowerShell Core versions/channels. Install `Splunk_TA_windows` (Splunkbase 742); restrict the search role because script text can contain credentials, tokens, paths or business logic.

Microsoft says Script Block Logging records processed commands, script blocks, functions and scripts. Windows PowerShell writes 4104 to `Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational`; PowerShell Core can use `PowerShellCore/Operational`. This rule pins the former. Invocation logging adds start/stop events and high volume and is not required. A `FromBase64String` match is an indicator, not proof.

## Enable, collect, verify

Govern **Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Windows PowerShell > Turn on PowerShell Script Block Logging** (or documented MDM equivalent). Computer policy takes precedence. Consider Microsoft's Protected Event Logging guidance and key-management implications. Configure `[WinEventLog://Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational]`, `renderXml=true`, `index=wineventlog`, `checkpointInterval=5` in managed `local/inputs.conf`.

Validate `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog`, exact source and fields:

```spl
index=wineventlog source="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational" EventCode=4104 earliest=-1h
| table _time Computer UserID ProcessID ScriptBlockId MessageNumber MessageTotal Path ScriptBlockText EventRecordID
```

Compare EventRecordIDs with Event Viewer. Verify fragment number/total and ScriptBlockId, preserve original Computer under WEF, prevent duplicate direct/forwarded collection, size channel/queues, and monitor source/policy health. Protect raw text and exports.

## Search and controls

Save `windows_powershell_4104_base64_decode`; schedule every five minutes for `earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m`. Measure latency and preserve nonoverlap. Hash complete observed fragment before creating a 240-character single-line preview. The regex is case-insensitive and identifies direct and reversed terms. It does not decode strings or reassemble fragments.

Replay positive and each negative fixture, including exact channel/ID, empty field, reverse term, latest boundary, hash determinism and no payload execution. Test multi-fragment scripts: a token split across fragments is a documented limitation; a controlled reconstruction search can group by host/ScriptBlockId and order MessageNumber only after proving complete MessageTotal. Record policy/add-on/Splunk/PowerShell versions, fixture, bounds, expected/actual rows, job ID and alert delivery. Keep draft until human acceptance.

## Triage and response

Verify policy/source freshness and raw fragment; recover all fragments with same host/ScriptBlockId; validate MessageNumber coverage; identify user/process/path and script signature/hash; correlate 4688/Sysmon parent/command line, module loads, child processes, network/DNS and EDR; determine deployment/management/response ownership; decode only in an isolated analysis environment with size/type limits and never execute output.

Do not automatically kill PowerShell, block the user, disable remoting, decode/render payloads in email, or suppress all signed/admin scripts. PowerShell can be legitimately used and compromised trusted infrastructure can run malicious code. Use approved EDR/account/network containment after corroboration.

## Troubleshooting

- No 4104: verify effective policy, new session after policy, exact Windows/PowerShell Core channel, input, index/RBAC and source health.
- Null ScriptBlockText/IDs: inspect raw XML and add-on knowledge; do not substitute generic Message without validation.
- Excessive volume: ensure invocation logging is not unnecessarily enabled; size retention/forwarding rather than dropping all 4104.
- Token split across fragments: reconstruct complete ordered ScriptBlockId after verifying all parts; document residual gaps.
- Frequent SCCM/module matches: hash/signature/job correlate and use exact bounded lookup exceptions.
- Alert text exposes secrets: remove previews from notifications, restrict dashboard/export and retain hashes/record IDs.
- Suspicious PowerShell without match: use broader Splunk/MITRE behavior analytics; this rule covers one decode primitive only.
grandmaExplanation: We look for PowerShell code that asks Windows to turn Base64 text back into bytes, a common step in both installers and hidden attack code. The alert preserves enough context for analysts to tell those apart without running the decoded material.
